title: Chapter 117
content:
Wei Wuxian had managed to dig up an ancient incense burner from the depths of the Ancient Chamber, the Lan Clan’s private treasury at the Cloud Recesses.

It was a curious little thing, sculpted like a chimera of wild beasts: the torso of a bear, an elephant's trunk, the eyes of a rhinoceros, an ox's tail, and the paws of a tiger. Its rounded belly served as the burner proper, puffing pale, fragrant curls of incense smoke from its gaping jaws.

Back in the Jingshi, Wei Wuxian turned the trinket over in his hands, examining it from every angle. "This thing looks fascinating. There’s no trace of killing intent or resentful energy clinging to it, so it definitely isn't cursed. Lan Zhan, do you have any idea what it’s actually for?"

Lan Wangji gave a slight shake of his head. Wei Wuxian leaned in to catch a whiff of the delicate fragrance drifting into the air; it smelled entirely harmless. Unable to puzzle out its secrets, they tucked the burner away, figuring they would investigate it properly another day.

Yet shortly after they turned in for the night, a heavy, suffocating exhaustion dragged them both under into a dead sleep. When Wei Wuxian finally blinked his eyes open, he found himself lying not on the soft linens of the Jingshi, but flat on the mossy floor of a wild mountain forest.

He pushed himself up on his elbows, brushing dry pine needles from his forearms. "Where the hell are we?"

Lan Wangji looked around with quiet composure. "We are not in the waking world."

"Not the waking world? Come on, you've got to be kidding me," Wei Wuxian laughed, giving his sleeves a sharp shake. The crisp mountain wind against his skin felt impossibly tangible. "If this isn't real, what is it?"

Without a word, Lan Wangji glided toward a nearby stream and gestured for him to look down into the shallows.

Wei Wuxian padded over and peered into the crystal-clear water. The breath caught in his throat.

Staring back up at him was his original face—the one from his past life!

His head snapped up in an instant. "It was that burner, wasn't it?"

"Most likely," Lan Wangji agreed with a nod.

Wei Wuxian stared at that long-lost reflection a moment longer, taking in the sharper jawline and familiar dark hair before tearing his eyes away. "Well, no need to panic. I already screened it earlier; there's zero malice in the craft. It's definitely not a demonic artifact, just some esoteric contraption an ancient grandmaster probably whipped up for meditation or idle amusement. Let’s scout the perimeter and get our bearings."

The two set off through the woods, wandering through what felt like an eerily vivid mirage. Before long, a rustic wooden hut came into view through the thinning trees.

Wei Wuxian pulled up short, letting out a sharp hum.

"What is it?" Lan Wangji asked.

Squinting through the foliage, Wei Wuxian tilted his head. "This place looks weirdly familiar."

It was an unassuming thatched cottage, the kind of humble farmstead scattered across any countryside, leaving him entirely unsure of where he could have ever seen it. Right at that moment, the rhythmic, wooden clatter of a working loom drifted out through the paper-pane windows.

Exchanging a glance, they closed the distance in silence.

Peeking over the threshold, both of them froze.

Whatever wild possibilities they had braced themselves for, reality blew right past them into utter absurdity. There were no ravenous ghouls, no lurking horrors, and no snarling fierce corpses. There was only a single man—one whose face they knew better than their own.

Sitting squarely inside the humble cottage was a second Lan Wangji!

This illusion of Lan Wangji possessed the exact same breathtaking features and tall, unyielding frame as the man standing beside him. He wore a simple, unadorned robe of homespun blue and white linen, yet the coarse fabric couldn't hide the effortless, untouchable poise of a highborn immortal. Beside him, the loom seemed to operate on unseen spiritual power, shuttling back and forth on its own in steady clatters. Meanwhile, the man himself sat poised by the window, entirely absorbed in a paper-bound scroll in his hands...

The real Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji had crossed the porch with barely a whisper of stealth, the floorboards groaning underfoot, yet the duplicate didn't so much as blink. Calm as still water, he casually turned a page with pale, slender fingers.

Wei Wuxian looked back and forth between the Lan Wangji at his side and the Lan Wangji at the desk. Light suddenly broke across his face. "I get it! Oh, I get it now!"

Lan Wangji’s brow twitched upward—a microscopic shift that signaled he was thoroughly baffled. "What do you understand?"

"This... this whole place is my dream!" Wei Wuxian crowed, clutching his ribs.

Right on cue, a lanky, dark-robed figure came ambling up the dirt path outside, his voice carrying through the trees in a lazy, playful drawl: "Er-gege, I'm ho-ome!"

Lan Wangji stared in stunned, stony silence as this dream-Wei Wuxian swung a hoe over one shoulder, swung a wicker fish basket from his other hand, and strutted inside with a blade of grass dangling cheekily between his teeth.

Naturally, if this was woven from Wei Wuxian’s subconscious, the phantoms living in it couldn't perceive their waking counterparts.

The Lan Wangji at the desk lifted his chin. Seeing his visitor, the corners of his mouth softened into a faint, fleeting smile before settling back into composure. He rose gracefully from his stool, walked over, and poured a cup of fresh spring water.

The dream-Wei Wuxian spat out the grass, collapsed onto a wooden bench, and took the cup, downing the water in three huge, noisy gulps. "The sun out there is brutal today," he groaned, wiping his mouth. "Practically fried me alive! I dumped all the chores in the dirt and called it a day. I'll finish the weeding whenever."

"Mn," the weaver hummed. He drew a pristine white towel from his sleeve to hand over, but the dream-Wei Wuxian simply thrust his grinning face forward, making his expectations shamelessly clear.

The duplicate didn't mind in the slightest; with meticulous, patient care, he began dabbing the sweat from his companion's brow.

Basking in the pampering, the phantom's mouth ran on without a break. "I went fooling around down by the creek earlier and snagged two fat carps! Er-gege, you’ve got to brew me some fish soup tonight!"

"Mn."

"How do Gusu folks usually cook carp anyway? Lan Zhan, do you know how to make that spicy pickled mustard fish? That's my absolute favorite. Just whatever you do, don't sweeten it. Had it that way once, nearly choked on the spot."

"Mn. I know how."

"It's getting muggy out, so we don't need the bathwater boiling hot tonight. That's why I only chopped half the firewood pile."

"Mn. It is fine."

Standing by the threshold, the real Lan Wangji watched the pair domesticate their way through the evening. "...This is your dream?"

Wei Wuxian was already laughing so hard his stomach was in knots. "Pffft—yeah! For a while back there, I kept having this exact same dream over and over! We gave up the cultivation world, ran off into the middle of nowhere to live like recluses. I'd go out hunting and farming, and you'd stay home weaving cloth, keeping house, and cooking my meals. Oh, and you balanced the accounts, handled the money, and mended my robes when they tore! Every single night, I dreamed about telling you to heat up the tub so we could bathe together, but right when we were about to strip, I'd wake up! What a rip-off, hahah!"

He didn't harbor an ounce of embarrassment about having his domestic daydreams laid bare; if anything, he looked thoroughly delighted with himself. Lan Wangji gazed at his wild, breathy laughter, his amber eyes softening with quiet warmth. "It sounds nice."

The dream was filled with nothing but trivial, everyday chores: chopping wood, feeding the yard chickens, simmering soup. True to Wei Wuxian’s word, the moment the steaming water filled the wooden tub, the illusion shattered into mist. Taking a few strides through the haze, the rustic cottage dissolved around them, replaced by an elegant, secluded pavilion framed by a sprawling magnolia tree whose ivory blossoms spilled their fragrance into the cool night air.

The setting had shifted entirely, landing them in a place neither of them could ever mistake: the Library Pavilion of the Cloud Recesses.

Up on the second floor, warm lamplight spilled through a latticed window, accompanied by the muffled scrape of furniture and faint voices. Wei Wuxian peered upward. "Shall we take a look?"

For some reason, Lan Wangji rooted his boots to the flagstones, uncharacteristically reluctant. He stared up at the glowing window, lost in heavy thought, looking distinctly hesitant. Wei Wuxian arched a brow, wondering what on earth could make Hanguang-jun drag his feet in his own home. "What's wrong?"

Lan Wangji gave a slight shake of his head. He parted his lips to answer, but before a word could form, a burst of uproarious, obnoxious laughter tore through the night.

Wei Wuxian's eyes sparked with instant recognition. Taking the stairs three at a time, he bounded into the pavilion.

Left with little choice, Lan Wangji trailed silently behind him. Slipping into the illuminated study, they were met with a sight that made Wei Wuxian stop in his tracks.

Sprawled across a pale woven mat by the punishment desk was a fifteen-year-old Wei Ying, slamming his palms against the low table as he howled with manic glee: "Ahaha!"

Tossed carelessly on the floor was a yellowed picture book. Standing huddled in the far corner of the room, looking like he’d just been cornered by a nest of vipers, was a teenage Lan Zhan, his pristine composure thoroughly shattered as he roared: "Wei Ying—!"

The younger Wei Ying was laughing so hard he rolled right under the writing desk, weakly hoisting a surrender flag with one waving hand. "Present! Sir, yes sir"

Standing off to the side, the adult Wei Wuxian was on the verge of collapsing from laughter himself, clinging to the real Lan Wangji's shoulder for dear life. "This dream is gold! Lan Zhan, look at you! Look at your face back then!"

Curiously enough, the real Lan Wangji's expression had turned deeply uncomfortable. Wei Wuxian pulled him down onto a nearby mat, propping his chin in his hand as he watched their younger selves bicker, squabble, and posture with absolute delight.

Second Young Master Lan! Mind your decorum! I brought my blade today—if we wreck this place, how are you explaining it to your uncle?!"

Lan Zhan’s chest heaved with fury. "What kind of creature are you?!"

Wei Ying gave a cheeky wag of his brows. "What kind do I look like? A red-blooded man!"

Watching the duel unfold, the adult Wei Wuxian let out a puzzled hum, tilting his head toward Lan Wangji. "Wait, did it go down like this? I could've sworn we didn't actually draw our swords that day."

Lan Wangji said nothing, deliberately avoiding his gaze. Wei Wuxian found his stiff silence increasingly suspicious, but before he could press the matter, the boy in the dream parried another strike, laughing mid-clash: "Not bad, Second Young Master! Great form, beautiful swordplay! But look at you, Lan Zhan—your cheeks are burning up! Are you flushed from the workout, or from that little masterpiece you just had your eyes on?"

You're way too green, kid."

Having swallowed his brazen insolence to the absolute breaking point, Lan Zhan finally snapped. Bichen flew from his hand in a ferocious arc; the impact tore both swords from their owners' grips, sending them clattering through the open window and down into the courtyard below.

Wei Ying blinked at his empty palms. "Hey, my sword!"

Still shouting, he made a break for the window to snatch his sword back, but Lan Zhan lunged from behind, tackling him straight to the floorboards.
